discussion.intro: Simpli is still new and benefits from broad discussion.
discussion.intro2: The choices we make—spelling, grammar, vocabulary—can be revisited with input from a large community. Below are some topics open for debate.
discussion.discordPlanned: Invite link: see Next steps (maintainers: set PUBLIC_DISCORD_INVITE_URL at build time).
discussion.governanceNote: How to propose changes: discuss publicly (Discord or forum), gather examples, then update the written spec when a decision is made.
discussion.communityBlurb: These topics are open for debate. Share your views and help shape Simpli.
discussion.topicChTitle: Removing « ch » and « c » (using « tj » for /tʃ/)
discussion.topicChDesc: Replacing ch with tj (e.g. child → tjaild, teacher → titjer) is a step toward simplicity and consistency—the letter c is one of the most inconsistent in English. It may, however, make Simpli feel less familiar to English speakers and could affect adoption. This is subject to discussion within the community.
discussion.topicVwTitle: V and W: keep both, fuse, or remove W?
discussion.topicVwDesc: Should we keep the sound /w/ (as in who, we, water) distinct from /v/? Fuse v and w into one letter (one sound, one spelling)? Or remove w entirely and use only v? Each choice affects simplicity, the size of the alphabet, and familiarity for English speakers and others.
discussion.topicProperNounsTitle: Proper nouns: keep as is or rewrite?
discussion.topicProperNounsDesc: Names of people, places, and brands: keep the original spelling (e.g. New York, Paris) or rewrite them in Simpli spelling (e.g. Niu York)? Keeping originals is recognizable but breaks the “one sound, one or two letters” rule; rewriting is consistent but can look unfamiliar. Open for community input.
discussion.topicPlaceNamesTitle: Geographical names: simplified Simpli spelling or each country’s romanization?
discussion.topicPlaceNamesDesc: For cities, countries, regions, and similar names, should we use one simplified Simpli form (consistent with Simpli phonics) or follow each place’s established romanization (official or widely used systems)? Simplified forms are uniform and easier to learn; classical or official spellings match maps, documents, and local usage but mix many conventions. Open for community input.

home.hero: Simpli is a simple international language: English-style words, Indonesian-style grammar, phonetic spelling.
home.concept1: Simpli is a simple international language—a proposed auxiliary language for egalitarian access to communication. It combines minimal grammar with familiar vocabulary so more people can use it quickly.
home.concept2: Whether you already know some English or are looking for a neutral bridge language, Simpli aims to reduce barriers of time, complexity, and geography.

grammarRulesPage.metaDescription: Full list of Simpli grammar rules.
grammarRulesPage.intro: Simpli has about 12 core rules. No conjugation, no gender, no cases.
grammarRulesPage.sectionPronounsBody: Simpli uses one word for all third-person singular: el. There is no separate “it”; el is used for he, she, and it (people and things). So el hav no hard gramer = It has no hard grammar; Yu kan lern el fast = You can learn it fast.
grammarRulesPage.sectionWordOrderBody: Subject – Verb – Object. Examples: mi si yu, wi it bred.
grammarRulesPage.sectionVerbsBody: Verbs never change. Express when with time words: yesterde, nao, tumoro. mi go, el go, dey go. Optionally use wil (future) or hav (past or perfect) before the main verb when no time word is given: mi wil go, mi hav finis. When a time word is present, wil and hav are optional and often omitted: tumoro mi go. Use olredi (already done) and stil (still ongoing): mi olredi finis, mi stil wok. hav also means “have” as a main verb (mi hav buk); context distinguishes auxiliary from main verb.
grammarRulesPage.sectionNegationBody: Put no before the verb: mi no go, el no si.
grammarRulesPage.sectionQuestionsBody: Start with wat, hu, wer, wen, wai, hao. hu means who; hao means how. Example: wat yu neim?
grammarRulesPage.sectionPluralBody: Optional. Use numbers or meni when needed: tu buk, meni haos.
grammarRulesPage.sectionAdjectivesBody: Before the noun, never change form: big haos, red buk.
grammarRulesPage.sectionPossessionBody: Noun + possessor: haos mi = my house, buk yu = your book. You can add of for clarity, but it’s not needed: haos (of) mi, haos (of) broder (of) mi = my brother’s house.
grammarRulesPage.sectionConnectorsBody: and, or, but, bikos, so. mi and yu, el no go bikos storm.
grammarRulesPage.sectionCompoundsBody: Join words with a hyphen when useful: sun-lait, fast-trein, woter-fud.

grammarPage.numbersBulletBody: Western digits (0–9); read aloud East Asian style (2026 → tu taosand tu ten siks). ISO dates; 24-hour clock.

grammarNumbers.intro: Write numbers with Western digits (0–9). When reading aloud, use East Asian–style composition: from large units to small, with tens built as digit + ten + digit (instead of a single word like “thirty-four”).
grammarNumbers.digits: Digits: sero (0), wan … nain (1–9), ten (10). Larger units: hundrad (hundred), taosand (thousand).

lessonsPage.title: Starter lessons
lessonsPage.intro: Short modules based on the site grammar and spelling pages. Simpli examples stay in Simpli; this UI is in your language.
lessonsPage.module1Body: Simpli uses Indonesian-style word order (SVO) and no verb conjugation. Time is expressed with words like yesterde, nao, tumoro—not by changing the verb. Without a time word, you may add wil (future) or hav (past or perfect); see the Time and aspect lesson.
lessonsPage.module2Body: Possession is noun + possessor: haos mi (my house), buk yu (your book).
lessonsPage.module3Body: A doubled vowel (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) may be used for extra clarity. In general, it is not: one vowel letter is enough.
lessonsPage.module4Body: Name the time with words like yesterde or tumoro—the verb stays the same. Without a time word, you may add wil (future) or hav (past or perfect). Use olredi for something already done and stil for something still going on.

samplesPage.whySimpliGloss: Simpli is a simple language. You can learn it fast. It has no hard grammar. Words come from English but the spelling is easy. Every sound has one or two letters. You read what you see. Many people in the world know some English. For them Simpli is a bridge. They can use it to talk to others. They can use it for work or travel. We want the world to have one simple language. Simpli can be that language.

roots.metaDescription: Simpli roots: real languages and current global usage.
roots.leadP: Simpli is not invented from scratch. It is rooted in real languages and current usage.
roots.grammarP: The grammar is inspired by Indonesian: analytic structure, no verb conjugation, no grammatical gender, optional plurals.
roots.vocabularyP: The vocabulary is based on English—simplified and regularized.
roots.whyP: Familiar vocabulary + minimal grammar = fast learning.
roots.spellingP: Regularized spelling also draws inspiration from Spanish. Spanish typically adapts loanwords to its own sound–letter norms instead of keeping English-style historical spellings—so almost any foreign word can be integrated cleanly. Simpli follows a similar idea. Example: football → futbol—the same kind of adaptation in Spanish and in Simpli.

comparison.metaDescription: Simpli vs Indonesian, English, Esperanto, Glosa, Globish.
comparison.intro: Simpli vs Indonesian, English, Esperanto, Glosa, Globish.
comparison.mediumH2: Medium: "Tomorrow, I will see you at my brother's house"
comparison.complexH2: More complex: "Next week I will go to the market to buy food for my family"
comparison.takeawayP: Takeaway: Simpli is simpler than Esperanto, more regular than English, more intuitive than Glosa.
comparison.notEnglishP: Simpli is not “simplified English.” It does not aim to replace English. You can still learn English and enjoy English literature and books while using Simpli as an auxiliary bridge language.

vocabulary.metaDescription: Simpli vocabulary: why English-based, core size, spelling, compounds.
vocabulary.leadP: Simpli vocabulary is based on English, simplified and written phonetically. Below we explain why we chose English rather than another language or invented words, then how the vocabulary works.
vocabulary.whyH2: Why English (and not another language or from scratch)?
vocabulary.whyLeadP: We use English-derived words for practical reasons, not because English is “better” or more neutral. The goal is to lower the barrier to a shared language.
vocabulary.whyBullet1: Already widely learned: More people learn English as a second language than any other. Hundreds of millions already know some English from school, work, or media. Using familiar roots gives them a head start instead of starting from zero.
vocabulary.whyBullet2: International use: English is already used in science, technology, business, and travel. Many terms (computer, hotel, internet, etc.) are already global. Simpli builds on that exposure so new words feel recognizable.
vocabulary.whyBullet3: Why not another language? Spanish, French, Mandarin, or Arabic are also global, but fewer people learn them as a second language worldwide. Choosing one of them would help some learners and leave others with no prior exposure. English, as the most common L2, gives the largest “transfer” benefit.
vocabulary.whyBullet4: Why not from scratch? A fully invented (a priori) vocabulary would be maximally neutral—no nation “owns” it—but it would be much harder to learn. There would be no cognates or familiar roots. Simpli prioritizes quick learnability so that more people can actually use it; English roots are a practical compromise.
vocabulary.whyCloseP: So: we use English as a base for recognition and speed, not as a statement that English is superior. The grammar is simplified and the spelling is regular, so Simpli is still its own system—just one that many can learn faster because the words look and sound familiar.
vocabulary.howBullet1: Core size: About 300–500 essential words for everyday use; the list can be extended as needed.
vocabulary.howBullet2: Spelling: One sound = one or two letters. See Spelling and Alphabet rationale.

specification.metaDescription: Official Simpli language specification: alphabet, spelling, grammar, vocabulary.
specification.leadP: This page links to the full, archived, numbered Simpli specification (for citation and long-term reference). Download the PDF below.
specification.livingP: The site also keeps the same material split into pages that may evolve over time:
specification.historyP: Distilled notes on why past design choices were made. If anything here disagrees with the current spec, follow the spec.

spellingBody.s1: Simpli uses phonetic spelling: one sound = one or two letters. No silent letters.
spellingBody.s2: One objective of this spelling is to help non-native speakers of English achieve clearer pronunciation—or at least to be more easily understood by both native and non-native listeners. Writing words as they are pronounced supports a more consistent accent and reduces misunderstandings.
spellingBody.s10: Consonants: p, b, t, d, k, g, m, n, f, s, l, r, h, v, w, y. No letter c (removed entirely). Use k for /k/. The sound /tʃ/ is written tj; /dʒ/ is written dj (symmetrical with tj). The [v]/[w] sound is written v (standard); w can still be used for familiarity with English. G always represents the hard /g/ sound (as in go, gud, giv, langwidj).
spellingBody.s29: English sounds that don’t exist in Simpli are mapped to the nearest letter:
spellingBody.s30: v / w — The [v] and [w] sounds are equivalent in Simpli. Use w when English spells the sound with w (at the start or inside the word): woter (water), watever (whatever), wi, windo. Use v when English uses v: seven, river, hav, giv, liv, mov, even. Speakers may pronounce either way. See Alphabet rationale for the full rule and examples.
spellingBody.s31: ch → tj (no letter c in Simpli): tjaild (child), titjer (teacher), tjeindj (change), tjis (cheese). For /k/ we always use k: skul (school), akson (action).
spellingBody.s35: ou → u — The sound is written u. Standard spelling is yu (you); you is acceptable for clarity or familiarity.
spellingBody.s37: Double consonants are not encouraged; they go against simplification. Prefer a single consonant: adres (not address). Double consonants are acceptable, but the simplified form is preferred.
spellingBody.s38: For simplification, Simpli spelling also avoids capital letters in regular words.
spellingBody.s40: A doubled vowel (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) may be used for extra clarity. In general, it is not: one vowel letter is enough.
spellingBody.s44: Every letter is pronounced. Spell the sound you hear:
spellingBody.s45: Diphthongs, one syllable each: /ai/ as ai (bai, tjaild), /ei/ as ei (plei), /au/ as ao (hao, nao), /oi/ as oi (boi, point). au is not used. Other vowel pairs, such as vidio, are two syllables.
spellingBody.s47: Syllables follow (C)V(C): consonant + vowel + optional consonant. Stress usually on the second-to-last syllable (kampyuter, yesterde, tumoro). The word list also keeps groups such as str and nk. Do not weaken the other vowels.
spellingBody.s51: How to define the spelling of a word
spellingBody.s52: Simpli spelling is based on pronunciation, not English spelling. Use this process:
spellingBody.s53: Start from pronunciation, not spelling. Convert the English word to its approximate phonemic form first.
spellingBody.s54:
Normalize the phoneme inventory. Apply Simpli sound decisions:
  • /θ/ → t
  • /ð/ → d
  • /tʃ/ → tj
  • /dʒ/ → dj
  • /k/ → k
  • /s/ → s
  • A doubled vowel (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) may be used for extra clarity. In general, it is not: one vowel letter is enough.
spellingBody.s55: Then write the Simpli spelling. Only after the sound has been identified.
spellingBody.s56: An automatic rule like “replace c with k” does not work, because English c can correspond to /k/, /s/, /tʃ/, or other sounds depending on the word. The same applies to g, x, th, and vowels. See Alphabet rationale for why letter-by-letter substitution fails and how to work from sounds instead.
spellingBody.s57: For easier adoption, Simpli targets strong simplification while avoiding major divergence from familiar English roots.
spellingBody.s58: Alphabet rationale — V and W, why we keep i and y, why automatic substitution fails, and full letter details.

alphabetRationale.metaDescription: V and W, why we keep i and y, full letter set, and spelling rules.
alphabetRationale.a1: This page explains the reasoning behind the Simpli alphabet: which letters we use, the V and W rule, and why we keep both i and y.
alphabetRationale.a3: Simpli uses a small, regular set of letters. Every sound is written with one or two letters; we avoid silent letters and extra symbols.
alphabetRationale.a4: Vowels: a, e, i, o, u. A doubled vowel (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) may be used for extra clarity. In general, it is not: one vowel letter is enough.
alphabetRationale.a5: Consonants: p, b, t, d, k, g, m, n, f, s, l, r, h, v, w, y. No letter c (removed entirely). Use k for /k/. The sound /tʃ/ is written tj; /dʒ/ is written dj (symmetrical with tj). G always represents the hard /g/ sound. The [v]/[w] sound is written w when English uses w, otherwise v.
alphabetRationale.a7: Use w when English spells the sound with w (at the start or inside the word). Use v when English uses v. Each letter has its own reference sound on the spelling page. Using one sound for both is widely understood, but then veri and weri, wi and vi, and van and wan sound the same.
alphabetRationale.a10: So: follow English w vs v spelling where that letter marks the [w]/[v] sound.
alphabetRationale.a12: We keep both i and y because they represent different sounds:
alphabetRationale.a13: i is a vowel (syllable nucleus): the sound in sit, see, it, eat. Examples: mi, bi, tri, faind, pipol, gud.
alphabetRationale.a14: y is a consonant (the glide [j]): the sound at the start of yes, you, year. Examples: yu, yes, yesterde, yelo (yellow). (The digraph dj is used for /dʒ/, a different sound.)
alphabetRationale.a15: i and y are two different sounds: a vowel and a consonant. Using y for [j] keeps spellings clear: yu (you) and yes are readable; iu or ies would blur the consonant with the vowel. So we keep both i and y.
alphabetRationale.a17: G always represents the hard /g/ sound (as in go, gud, giv, langwidj). It never represents the /dʒ/ sound that English uses in words like “giant” or “general”. dj represents /dʒ/ (symmetrical with tj for /tʃ/): djob, djeneral, djaiant, meidjer, bridj. This contrast makes pronunciation predictable.
alphabetRationale.a19: Simpli also drops or maps other English letters to keep the alphabet small and phonetic:
alphabetRationale.a20: c — not used in Simpli. We use k for /k/ (e.g. skul, akson). The sound /tʃ/ is written tj; /dʒ/ is written dj: tjaild (child), titjer (teacher), tjeindj (change), tjis (cheese), djob, bridj (bridge).
alphabetRationale.a22: Why the automatic c → k rule fails
alphabetRationale.a23: Because English c can correspond to different sounds:
alphabetRationale.a26: electric → final c is /k/, but not every c in English is
alphabetRationale.a27: So the real rule is not “replace c with k,” but:
alphabetRationale.a28: and sometimes other outcomes depending on actual pronunciation
alphabetRationale.a35: So a serious Simpli corpus cannot be built from raw orthographic substitutions alone. You must start from pronunciation, then apply the Simpli phoneme inventory (see Spelling → “How to define the spelling of a word”).
alphabetRationale.a36: For long vowels, syllable rules, and common endings, see Spelling.

numbersBody.n1: Simpli uses Western digits (0–9) for writing numbers, dates, and times—the same numerals used internationally with the Latin alphabet. When you read numbers aloud, build them East Asian style: from large units to small, with tens as digit + ten + digit. Dates follow the international ISO format; months use international English names in Simpli spelling. Clock time uses the 24-hour system (no AM/PM).
numbersBody.n3: Write numbers with the ten standard digits:
numbersBody.n4: Use digits in dates (2026-06-18), times (14:30), prices, and most formal text. Saying a number aloud uses Simpli words (below), not the digit names in English.
numbersBody.n6: Name units from large to small, like Thai, Lao, Chinese, and Japanese—not like English “twenty twenty-six.”
numbersBody.n7: Tens are built as digit + ten + digit (not a single word like “thirty-four”). For 10–19, omit the leading wan: 14 = ten for (ten-four), not wan ten for.
numbersBody.n10: 100 → wan hundrad (one hundred; or just hundrad when clear)
numbersBody.n11: Digit words: sero (0), wan (1), tu (2), tri (3), for (4), faiv (5), siks (6), seven (7), eit (8), nain (9), ten (10).
numbersBody.n13: Context distinguishes tu (two) from the preposition tu (to), and for (four) from the preposition for.
numbersBody.n15: Written format (preferred): international ISO YYYY-MM-DD with digits and hyphens.
numbersBody.n16: Prose format: day, then month name, then year—common internationally:
numbersBody.n17: Read aloud: use compositional numbers for the day and year; use the month name or month number:
numbersBody.n18: 2026-06-18 (ISO) → year, month, day: tu taosand tu ten siks, siks (month 06), wan ten eit
numbersBody.n20: Simpli spelling of each month, next to the name in your language:
numbersBody.n25: Use the 24-hour clock. There is no AM/PM.
numbersBody.n26: Written format:HH:MM with digits and a colon (or hyphen when a colon is awkward):
numbersBody.n27: Read aloud: say the hour, then the minutes—either compactly or with unit words. For hours 10–19, omit the leading wan (like East Asian and Chinese): 14 = ten for, not wan ten for.
numbersBody.n28: 14:30 → ten for ten tri or ten for aoer tri ten minat
numbersBody.n32: See also grammar rules for time words with verbs (yesterde, nao, tumoro).

grammarOverview.lead: Simpli uses an analytic grammar inspired by Indonesian.
grammarOverview.bulletPronouns: Pronouns: One word for he, she, and it: el. Simpli does not have a separate “it”; el is used for all third-person singular (people and things). So: el go = he/she/it goes, El hav no hard gramer = It has no hard grammar.
grammarOverview.bulletVerbs: Verbs: Never change form. Time with words (yesterde, nao, tumoro). Optionally wil / hav for future or past when no time word; olredi / stil for completed or ongoing.
grammarOverview.bulletPossession: Possession: Noun + possessor: haos mi = my house. You can add of for clarity, but it’s not needed: haos (of) mi, haos (of) broder (of) mi = my brother’s house.
grammarOverview.bulletQuestions: Questions: Start with wat, hu, wer, wen, wai, hao.

motivation.intro: Simpli is a simple international language—why does it matter? Egalitarian access to communication matters. Today, the languages that open doors (English, Mandarin, Spanish) require years of study and often reflect historical power rather than fairness.
motivation.positioningQuote: Simpli is a next-generation auxiliary language combining English vocabulary with Indonesian-style grammar to achieve maximum simplicity without sacrificing expressiveness.
motivation.notSimplifiedEnglish: Simpli is not “simplified English.” Simpli does not aim to replace English. You can still learn English and enjoy English literature and books while using Simpli as an auxiliary bridge language.
motivation.time: Time: Learn the basics in weeks, not years.
motivation.complexity: Complexity: No conjugation, no gender, minimal grammar.
motivation.neutrality: Neutrality: This standard is for everyone to read and speak.
motivation.pronunciation: Pronunciation: Phonetic spelling helps non-native speakers be more easily understood by both native and non-native listeners.
motivation.bridge: A language that many people can learn quickly can serve as a bridge for work, travel, and cooperation, without requiring everyone to master a complex historical national language.
motivation.strategicLearning: Learning speed: basics can be acquired quickly.
motivation.strategicFamiliarity: Potential global familiarity: English-rooted vocabulary supports recognition.
motivation.scalabilityIntro: Simpli has strong potential to become a real language if:
motivation.scalabilityGrammar: the grammar is complete, not only minimal,
motivation.scalabilityRules: the rules remain closed and stable,
motivation.scalabilityCommunity: the community can extend vocabulary coherently.
motivation.scalabilityRisk: Key risk: if spelling diverges too far from English, Simpli loses a major advantage for adoption.
